entries_new.name: Paulet affair (British occupation of Hawaii, 1843)
entries_new.stopped_by: Rear-Admiral Richard Thomas, with US warships present
entries_new.challenge: Hawaiian government; American naval officers; the British Admiralty
entries_new.mechanism: A naval captain acting without orders from London forced a cession of disputed land and ran the government under a commission.
entries_new.story: In February 1843 Captain Lord George Paulet of the Royal Navy ship HMS Carysfort sailed into Honolulu and demanded that King Kamehameha III meet him, backing a dispute about land claimed by the British consul Richard Charlton. Under threat of attack the Hawaiian government signed over the disputed land under protest on 25 February. Paulet set up a commission of himself and three others as government and raised the British flag. London had not authorised this. Rear-Admiral Richard Thomas arrived on 26 July and ended the occupation on 31 July 1843, after American warships had also reached Honolulu. The date is now a Hawaiian holiday.

entries_new.name: William Astor Chanler's 1902 Venezuela insurrection
entries_new.stopped_by: Called off after Castro agreed to honour his loan terms
entries_new.challenge: Government of Venezuela under Cipriano Castro
entries_new.mechanism: Foreign creditors paid for an armed landing meant to force or replace a debtor government.
entries_new.story: In 1902 Dutch investors who feared that Venezuelan President Cipriano Castro would default on a large loan approached the American former congressman William Astor Chanler and asked him to stage a rebellion. According to his Wikipedia biography, he raised a small army of adventurers, which landed on the Venezuelan coast and marched inland. The rising was called off when Castro agreed to comply with the terms of his loans. Chanler later borrowed funds for a water and sewage project in Tampico, Mexico, and published a fictionalised account of the episode in 1921 under the pen name John Brent.

entries_new.name: Chatham Roberdeau Wheat's expeditions
entries_new.mechanism: Private soldier-for-hire commanding volunteers in other countries' conflicts.
entries_new.story: Chatham Roberdeau Wheat was a Louisiana lawyer and legislator who, after the Mexican-American War, served as a fighter for hire in several foreign campaigns. He held a colonel's commission from Narciso Lopez in the Cuban filibustering expeditions (private armies raised in the United States to invade a foreign country). In 1855 the State of Guerrero in Mexico made him a brigadier general of artillery in the campaign of Juan Alvarez against Santa Anna. He then went to Italy to serve under Garibaldi but left when Virginia seceded. He raised the Louisiana Tigers battalion for the Confederacy and died in June 1862.

entries_new.name: Aunus expedition (Finnish volunteers in Olonets Karelia)
entries_new.founder: Gunnar von Hertzen, later Aarne Sihvo
entries_new.stopped_by: Soviet Red Army and Red Guard counterattack; Treaty of Tartu border
entries_new.mechanism: Volunteer army seeking to occupy a neighbouring region and attach it to Finland.
entries_new.story: In April 1919 about a thousand Finnish volunteers crossed into Olonets Karelia, which Finns call Aunus, a Russian-ruled area inhabited mostly by Finnic-language people. The aims were Lodeynoye Pole, Petrozavodsk and the Murmansk railway. A second recruitment of 2,000 volunteers followed, but few local Karelians joined. A Red Army landing at Vitele on 26 June forced the Finns back. Under the 1920 Treaty of Tartu the border was drawn with Repola and Porajarvi on the Soviet side, and Finnish troops left by February 1921. The expedition was one of several Finnish 'kinship wars' of the period.

entries_new.name: Falke expedition (Cumana landing, 1929)
entries_new.mechanism: Exile junta tried to land an armed force from a ship to overthrow a dictator.
entries_new.story: On 11 August 1929 the steamship Falke, renamed General Anzoategui for the occasion, entered the Venezuelan port of Cumana carrying 250 to 300 men led by the former admiral Roman Delgado Chalbaud. Exiles in Paris had formed a Junta de Liberacion Nacional to oust President Juan Vicente Gomez. Venezuelan forces met the ship. Delgado was killed on the first day, and the expedition's leaders surrendered on 24 August. His son Carlos escaped. The Venezuelan envoy in Europe, Jose Ignacio Cardenas, had reported the plan, which helped defeat it.

entries_new.name: Northern Autonomous Zone of Junbish-e Milli
entries_new.stopped_by: Taliban capture in 1998; later absorbed into the Afghan state
entries_new.challenge: Rival Afghan factions, the Taliban, and later the central government
entries_new.mechanism: A former army division kept its territory when the national government collapsed.
entries_new.story: From 1992 the Uzbek-led Junbish-e Milli movement under Abdul Rashid Dostum held seven provinces of northern Afghanistan around Mazar-e-Sharif, with about five million people according to Wikipedia. It had its own airline, Balkh Airlines, printed its own currency, had a foreign minister and drew electricity from Uzbekistan. The Taliban took Mazar-e-Sharif in August 1998 and Dostum fled. He returned in 2001 and the zone became part of the new Islamic Republic of Afghanistan in law while he kept control in practice. The last report that he controlled the city is dated 4 November 2007.

entries_new.name: Tocoron prison and Tren de Aragua
entries_new.founder: Hector Rusthenford Guerrero Flores and others
entries_new.challenge: Venezuelan security forces; US executive designation and court challenges
entries_new.mechanism: A prison run from inside by a criminal group served as its base.
entries_new.story: Tren de Aragua is a Venezuelan criminal group that Wikipedia says began inside the Tocoron prison in Aragua state, where its leader Hector Guerrero Flores was held from 2013 to 2023. The prison served as the group's de facto headquarters until Venezuelan security forces took it over in a 2023 raid, after which the leadership escaped. In February 2025 the United States designated the group a Foreign Terrorist Organization and cited the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 for deportations; that order was challenged in court, and some experts dispute the terrorist label, describing the group as money-driven. Guerrero is reported to have died in June 2026.

entries_new.name: Pailin, Khmer Rouge stronghold
entries_new.stopped_by: Surrender of the Ieng Sary faction in 1996; integration under the Cambodian government
entries_new.mechanism: A retreating movement held a resource-rich border district funded by gem and timber extraction.
entries_new.story: Pailin, a gem-mining district in western Cambodia near the Thai border, was captured by the Khmer Rouge on 20 April 1975. After Vietnamese forces ousted the Khmer Rouge in 1979 the movement retreated there, and Wikipedia says it held the area long afterwards and used it as the capital of its Provisional Government of National Union and National Salvation of Cambodia from 1994 to 1998. The Ieng Sary faction surrendered in 1996, and Pailin was separated from Battambang province. Prime Minister Hun Sen's government let former members manage it as a special administrative area to keep the peace.

entries_new.name: Sheng Shicai's rule of Xinjiang
entries_new.stopped_by: Removal by the Chinese national government in August 1944
entries_new.challenge: Ma Zhongying, Zhang Peiyuan, the Chinese national government
entries_new.mechanism: A provincial commander held power by a Soviet military alliance, then tried to switch patrons.
entries_new.story: Sheng Shicai became military governor of Xinjiang after a coup on 12 April 1933 and ruled until August 1944. He defeated rivals Ma Zhongying and Zhang Peiyuan by June 1934 after inviting Soviet troops to intervene, and in return subordinated the province to Moscow; the Soviets held a monopoly on Xinjiang trade and extracted oil and rare materials. Wikipedia reports a purge in 1937 that executed, tortured to death or imprisoned 100,000 people. He expelled Soviet personnel in July 1942, tried to switch sides again in 1944, and was removed by the Chinese government, which made him a minister.

entries_new.name: AUC-held areas of Uraba and the Santa Fe de Ralito zone
entries_new.founder: Coalition of paramilitary groups organised through the ACCU
entries_new.stopped_by: Demobilisation talks with the Uribe government, 2003 to 2006
entries_new.challenge: FARC and ELN; designated a terrorist organisation by the US, Canada and the EU
entries_new.mechanism: A paramilitary coalition held districts by force, with believed links to some local army commanders, and later negotiated a safe-haven zone.
entries_new.story: The United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia (AUC) was a coalition of paramilitary groups formed in April 1997 by merging local militias, active in the Colombian conflict until 2006. Wikipedia says it had about 20,000 members, financed by the drug trade and landowners. In Uraba, in northern Antioquia, it dislodged the FARC and gained what the article calls total control in the mid to late 1990s. In May 2004 the government granted its leaders and 400 bodyguards a 368 km2 zone at Santa Fe de Ralito, Cordoba, in which arrest warrants would not apply during talks. Most blocs demobilised by early 2006.
entries_new.anchor: Santa Fe de Ralito, Cordoba, Colombia

sources.t: Wikipedia: United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia

entries_new.name: French protectorate of Cambodia
entries_new.challenge: Revolt of 1885 to 1887 led by Si Votha
entries_new.mechanism: A king traded foreign affairs and defence to France in exchange for keeping his throne.
entries_new.story: On 11 August 1863 King Norodom of Cambodia signed a treaty accepting a French protectorate. He had asked for it, as Cambodia was then a vassal of Siam and was threatened by Vietnam, and the French governor of Cochinchina saw it as a buffer. The monarchy stayed but power passed largely to a resident general in Phnom Penh, and France took over foreign and trade relations and defence. Siam recognised the arrangement after France ceded Battambang and accepted Thai control of Angkor. Cambodia joined French Indochina in 1887, became self-ruling in 1947 and an associated state in 1949, and gained full independence on 9 November 1953.

entries_new.name: Federated Malay States (British protected Malay states)
entries_new.founder: British government and the four Malay rulers
entries_new.mechanism: Rulers accepted British Residents by treaty, and the four states were pooled under a British resident-general.
entries_new.story: In 1874 the Sultan of Perak signed the Treaty of Pangkor, agreeing to accept a British Resident whose advice must be followed on everything except Malay religion and custom. The system spread to Selangor and Negeri Sembilan that year and to Pahang in 1888. The Treaty of Federation of 1895, effective 1 July 1896, joined the four states as the Federated Malay States, with real power held by a resident-general. A Federal Council was created in 1909. The Unfederated Malay States kept more internal autonomy. The federation ended in 1946 when the states joined the Malayan Union, which became the Federation of Malaya in 1948.

entries_new.name: French protectorate of Laos
entries_new.challenge: Siam (protest, then forced to recognise); Lao Issara government 1945 to 1946
entries_new.mechanism: A weakened vassal king requested protection from a colonial power.
entries_new.story: After the Black Flag Army, bands from China, sacked the capital of Luang Phrabang in 1888, King Oun Kham asked for French protection. A bill designating the kingdom a protectorate was signed on 27 March 1889 despite Siamese protest. In 1893 France sent warships to Bangkok in the Paknam incident, and Siam recognised French control of the east bank of the Mekong. Nominal rule stayed with the king, but power lay with a French governor. Phuan (1899) and Champasak (1904) were annexed into it and ruled directly. After a brief Japanese-backed state in 1945, the Kingdom of Laos became an associated state in 1949 and independent in 1953.

entries_new.name: Qatar under British protection, 1916 to 1971
entries_new.stopped_by: End of the British treaty relationship; independence declared 3 September 1971
entries_new.mechanism: A ruler gave Britain control over territory transfers and foreign relations in return for naval protection.
entries_new.story: In 1916 Qatar became a British protectorate when Abdullah Al Thani signed a treaty saying he could cede territory only to Britain, in return for protection from attack by sea and support if attacked by land. A 1934 treaty gave more extensive protection. A 75-year oil concession followed in 1935, and oil was found at Dukhan in 1940. In 1968 Britain announced it would end its treaty relationships with the Gulf sheikhdoms, and Qatar joined eight other protected states in planning a federation of Arab emirates. The nine could not agree terms, and Qatar declared independence on 3 September 1971.

entries_new.name: Sultanate of Egypt, British protectorate 1914 to 1922
entries_new.challenge: Egyptian nationalist movement and the 1919 uprising
entries_new.mechanism: Britain ended nominal Ottoman rule and held real power through officials beside a sultan it installed.
entries_new.story: After the First World War began, Britain removed Khedive Abbas II of Egypt for pro-Ottoman positions and replaced him with his uncle Hussein Kamel, who declared Egypt independent of the Ottoman Empire and took the title Sultan. The new sultanate was a British protectorate, with real political and military power held by British officials. Wartime British requisitions and the conscription of 55,000 Egyptians for labor corps caused resentment. When the nationalist Wafd delegation led by Saad Zaghlul was refused travel to London and Zaghlul was deported to Malta in March 1919, a nationwide uprising followed. The protectorate ended with the Declaration of Egyptian Independence of 1922.

entries_new.name: Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia
entries_new.challenge: Czechoslovak government in exile; Munich Agreement terms
entries_new.mechanism: A German-protected autonomous territory with a dual legal system set up after occupation.
entries_new.story: After the Slovak Republic declared independence on 14 March 1939 and German troops occupied the Czech rump state the next day, Hitler proclaimed the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia from Prague Castle on 16 March 1939. President Emil Hacha had accepted Hitler's request for the occupation in Berlin. Wikipedia notes the move violated the Munich Agreement. The protectorate was nominally autonomous, with German law applying to ethnic Germans and a Czech administration, described as puppet, governing the other residents. Germany seized the Czechoslovak central bank's gold and currency reserves. It ended with Germany's surrender in May 1945.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia

entries_new.name: Monaghan Asylum Soviet
entries_new.mechanism: Workers declared control of their workplace during a strike.
entries_new.story: On 29 January 1919 staff at the Monaghan Lunatic Asylum, now St. Davnet's Hospital, declared a soviet (a workers' council taking over a workplace) as part of a strike, led by the union organiser and IRA commander Peadar O'Donnell. Complaints included a 93-hour working week and a ban on leaving the premises between shifts. A red flag was flown, and workers barricaded themselves in when armed police arrived. The operators negotiated. Workers won a 56-hour week and a pay rise, and married staff could go home after shifts. It was disestablished on 4 February. This was the first of the Irish soviets.

entries_new.name: Knocklong Soviet Creamery
entries_new.founder: Irish Transport and General Workers Union members
entries_new.stopped_by: Negotiated settlement; creamery burned by Black and Tans, August 1920
entries_new.mechanism: Workers occupied and operated their employer's plants.
entries_new.story: On 15 May 1920 workers belonging to the Irish Transport and General Workers Union seized creameries in County Limerick owned by the Cleeve family, the main one near Knocklong, and ran them without the owners. A banner on the building said the workers made butter, not profits. After five days the Cleeves agreed to a wage increase, a 48-hour week, 14 holidays a year and better ventilation. The Cleeves insured the creamery against fire on 24 August 1920, and on 26 August Black and Tans burned it down.

entries_new.name: Waterford Soviet
entries_new.mechanism: Strikers ran a permit system in the city during a general strike.
entries_new.story: In April 1920 a soviet arose in Waterford City during a national general strike for the release of Republican hunger strikers. Workers enforced the strike and ran a permit system. After some days the strike was reported a success and thousands gathered at City Hall, where union leaders sang The Red Flag. Irish papers gave it little attention, since nationalists did not want to feed loyalist claims that Sinn Fein was Bolshevik, and the soviets did not try to change the social order. Newspapers in Britain wrote of 'Red Guards' and a 'Soviet Commissioner', and said a red flag flew over the town hall.

entries_new.name: Bruree Soviet
entries_new.mechanism: Workers occupied a mill and set their own prices.
entries_new.story: On 26 August 1921 nearly all employees of the Cleeve family's bakery and mills in Bruree, County Limerick, occupied them, leaving only the manager and a clerk. They raised a red flag and a banner reading 'Bruree Soviet Workers Mill', and said they would sell food at lower prices. Union officials claimed they cut prices, doubled sales and raised wages. The owners were forced into negotiations at Liberty Hall in Dublin, mediated by Countess Markievicz, Sinn Fein's Minister for Labour, who it is alleged threatened to send IRA troops if the workers refused the arbitration.

entries_new.name: Cork Harbour Soviet
entries_new.founder: Irish Transport and General Workers Union branch
entries_new.mechanism: Workers seized a public building to force a wage claim.
entries_new.story: A commission set up by Lord Mayor Tomas Mac Curtain recommended in 1920 a living wage of 70 shillings a week for Cork workers. The Cork Harbour Board rejected it repeatedly, finally in September 1921. Workers then seized the Cork Custom House, flew a red flag and declared a soviet on 7 September 1921. The New York Times reported it, and The Irish Times called it an outbreak of 'Irish Bolshevism'. The soviet ended with an agreement on a wage increase.

entries_new.name: La Familia Michoacana in Michoacan
entries_new.founder: Carlos Rosales Mendoza; Nazario Moreno Gonzalez was its second leader
entries_new.stopped_by: Death of Moreno Gonzalez and a split into successor groups; capture of Mendez Vargas in 2011
entries_new.mechanism: A cartel gained influence over local politics and offered to stand down in return for state security guarantees.
entries_new.story: La Familia Michoacana is a Mexican drug cartel based in Michoacan that split from the Gulf Cartel and Los Zetas in 2006. Wikipedia reports that it became involved in the state's politics, backing candidates, financing campaigns and pressing other parties to withdraw candidates. In July 2009 and November 2010 it offered to retreat and even disband if federal and state police committed to the safety of Michoacan. President Felipe Calderon's government refused to negotiate. Its leader Nazario Moreno Gonzalez was reported killed on 9 December 2010, a death the same source also calls alleged, and leaders split off to form the Knights Templar Cartel and La Nueva Familia Michoacana. Mexico's Attorney General reported the cartel exterminated by 2011, while the same source says it still existed that year in Estado de Mexico.

entries_new.name: Rafael Simon Urbina's raids on Gomez's Venezuela, 1929 and 1931
entries_new.stopped_by: Venezuelan forces under General Leon Jurado
entries_new.mechanism: Exile bands crossed the sea by seized ship or landing to try to overthrow a dictator.
entries_new.story: Rafael Simon Urbina, a Venezuelan rebel against dictator Juan Vicente Gomez, led about 250 men in 1929 in taking Fort Amsterdam on the Dutch island of Curacao and kidnapping the Dutch governor, Leonard Albert Fruytier. They took weapons, ammunition and the island's treasury and sailed to Venezuela on the stolen American ship Maracaibo. They landed at La Vela de Coro, in Falcon State, and General Leon Jurado's forces defeated them. In October 1931 Urbina landed at Puerto Gutierrez with 137 Mexican laborers and eight Venezuelans, captured Capatarida, and was defeated again by Jurado.
entries_new.anchor: La Vela de Coro, Falcon State, Venezuela

entries_new.name: Black Sea mutiny of the French Navy, 1919
entries_new.founder: Andre Marty and other crew leaders
entries_new.mechanism: Crews refused orders and flew a red flag on their ships.
entries_new.story: In 1919 crews of French warships sent to the Black Sea to support the White side in the Russian Civil War mutinied against that policy. The first mutiny began on 16 April on the destroyer Protet, anchored at the Danube port of Galatz, and spread to ships stationed in Crimea. On 20 April a red flag was raised, without lowering the French tricolour, on the battleships Jean Bart and France. The cruiser Waldeck-Rousseau joined on 23 April. Causes included poor conditions and no demobilisation after the armistice. A court-martial in Constantinople in July 1919 sentenced Andre Marty to 20 years of forced labor. About 100 sailors were sentenced; most were soon reprieved.

entries_new.name: Lurongyu 2682 trawler mutiny, 2011
aka: Mutiny and mass murder on Lurongyu 2682
entries_new.challenge: Ship captain and company; Chinese courts
entries_new.mechanism: Crew took command of a fishing vessel during a contract dispute.
entries_new.story: Lurongyu 2682 was a Chinese squid-fishing trawler registered in Rongcheng, Shandong. On 16 June 2011, in the South Pacific, a group of 11 crewmen led by Liu Guiduo seized it from Captain Li Chengquan. They said they wanted to return to China, and the contract papers the company had given them carried a forged stamp. Of 33 men aboard, 16 were killed and 6 jumped overboard and are presumed dead, according to Wikipedia. Eleven crew returned to China and were convicted of murder in 2013, five with death sentences, including the captain. The captain had cooperated in a later stage, when the mutineers persuaded him to sail toward Japan.

entries_new.name: Cocos Islands mutiny, 1942
entries_new.mechanism: Garrison soldiers tried to seize an island group to hand it to an enemy power.
entries_new.story: On the night of 8 May 1942, 30 of 56 Ceylon Garrison Artillery soldiers on Horsburgh Island in the Cocos (Keeling) Islands mutinied against their British officers. According to Wikipedia, they intended to hand the islands to the Japanese, who had occupied Christmas Island on 31 March. The plan to arrest the officers and turn the 6-inch guns on loyal troops failed, and one gunner was killed. Other Ceylonese infantry on Direction Island helped to put the mutiny down. Three ringleaders were sentenced to death, the only British Commonwealth servicemen executed for mutiny in the Second World War.

entries_new.name: HMS Dominica mutiny, 1806
entries_new.mechanism: Crew took a naval schooner and handed it to an enemy navy.
entries_new.story: HMS Dominica was a schooner bought by the Royal Navy in 1805. In 1806 her crew mutinied and turned her over to the French, who sent her out as the privateer Napoleon (a privately owned armed ship licensed to attack enemy shipping). Within four days HMS Wasp had recaptured her. She went back into British service under her original name and was broken up in 1808. A list of mutinies on Wikipedia adds that the ringleader was hanged. The mutiny took place in the Caribbean, but the sources read do not give the exact place.
entries_new.anchor: Caribbean, near Dominica (exact place not given)

entries_new.name: Leoncavallo self-managed social centre, Milan
entries_new.founder: Squatters who occupied the Scotti factory in 1975
entries_new.challenge: City of Milan, property owners, the Italian government
entries_new.mechanism: Squatters took over an empty industrial building and ran it as a self-financed public space.
entries_new.story: Centro Sociale Leoncavallo was a self-managed social centre in Milan, begun in 1975 when squatters occupied a former pharmaceutical factory on via Leoncavallo. The city evicted it in 1989 and the building was partly demolished, but it was reoccupied within days and rebuilt by hand. A 1994 eviction followed, and the centre moved to a warehouse for some months and then to a former printing works on via Watteau. Activities included concerts, theatre, language courses and a radio station, and by 2003 about 80 people worked there. It refused to pay taxes. Authorities evicted it from via Watteau on 21 August 2025.

entries_new.name: Staatenbund Osterreich (Austrian Commonwealth)
entries_new.mechanism: Declared a parallel state with its own documents and sought to replace the government.
entries_new.story: Staatenbund Osterreich, meaning Austrian Commonwealth, was a group in Austria set up in November 2015. It issued its own passports and licence plates, had a written constitution and used language from the One People's Public Trust. In 2019 its leader was sentenced to 14 years in prison for trying to order the army to overthrow the government and for asking Vladimir Putin for foreign help. Other members received shorter sentences.

entries_new.name: Wieambilla shootings, Queensland, 2022
entries_new.story: On 12 December 2022 two Queensland police constables, Matthew Arnold and Rachel McCrow, and a neighbour, Alan Dare, were killed at a rural property at Wieambilla, 270 km northwest of Brisbane. The three residents, brothers Gareth and Nathaniel Train and Gareth's wife Stacey, were later shot dead by police. Gareth Train was an online conspiracy theorist who supported the sovereign citizen movement. A coronial inquest found it did not meet the legal definition of a terror act and attributed it to a shared psychosis rooted in religious beliefs. ASIO and the Australian Federal Police later said they would examine sovereign citizen groups more closely.

entries_new.name: Mutiny on Henry Hudson's Discovery, 1611
entries_new.founder: Mutineers named by Pricket as Henry Greene and Robert Juet
entries_new.mechanism: Crew took the ship from its captain and sailed home.
entries_new.story: In June 1611, after wintering on the shore of James Bay, most of the crew of the English ship Discovery mutinied against Henry Hudson, who wanted to keep exploring west for a Northwest Passage. The mutineers cast Hudson, his son and six others adrift in a small boat, and the eight were never seen again by Europeans. Only eight of the thirteen mutinous crewmen survived the voyage home. They were arrested in England and some were tried, but no punishment was imposed for the mutiny. Wikipedia notes that accounts come only from mutineers, notably Abacuk Pricket, and that historians question his reliability.

entries_new.name: ICJ advisory opinion on the Wall in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, 2004
entries_new.challenge: Israel argued the Court should decline to rule and that the barrier was needed for security
entries_new.mechanism: A court opinion that a barrier built inside occupied territory breaches international law.
entries_new.story: On 9 July 2004 the International Court of Justice gave a non-binding advisory opinion, requested by the UN General Assembly on 8 December 2003, on the barrier Israel is building in and around the West Bank. The Court held, by 14 votes to 1, that the sections inside the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and the permit regime breach Israel's obligations under international law, and that the barrier should be torn down. It held that Israel owes reparation and that self-defence and necessity could not be invoked for the route. The Assembly endorsed the findings on 20 July 2004 by 150 votes to 6.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Legal Consequences of the Construction of a Wall in the Occupied Palestinian Territory

entries_new.name: Mary of Burgundy and her marriage to Maximilian, 1477
entries_new.founder: Charles the Bold (father); Mary of Burgundy
entries_new.recognition: Accepted as ruler in several domains; not recognised by Louis XI
entries_new.mechanism: An heiress kept a state by marrying into a powerful dynasty.
entries_new.story: Mary of Burgundy, only child of Charles the Bold, became ruler of the Valois-Burgundian lands at 19 after her father died at the Battle of Nancy on 5 January 1477. King Louis XI of France did not recognise her claims and seized the Duchy of Burgundy and the Free County of Burgundy, which led to the War of the Burgundian Succession. She married Maximilian of Austria, son of Emperor Frederick III, to gain Habsburg support. They secured much of the Burgundian Netherlands but could not recover the lands Louis had taken. After she died in a riding accident in 1482, her son Philip the Handsome inherited her titles and claims.

entries_new.name: Ismail Khan's Herat (the "Emir of Herat")
entries_new.stopped_by: Removal by President Karzai and pressure from rival commanders, March 2004
entries_new.challenge: Afghan Transitional Administration under Hamid Karzai
entries_new.mechanism: A provincial governor kept customs revenue and an armed force outside central control.
entries_new.story: After the Taliban fell in December 2001, Ismail Khan, a former mujahideen commander, again became governor of Herat in western Afghanistan. Wikipedia reports that he took control of the city from the local religious scholars, held the trade route to Iran as a main source of revenue, and was called Emir of Herat. He was accused of human rights abuses and of ruling like a private fiefdom. He refused to pass customs revenue from Iran and Turkmenistan to the national government. President Karzai removed him from his army command in August 2003, and rival commanders and the central government forced him out in March 2004.

entries_new.name: Kuomintang army in the Shan States of Burma
entries_new.stopped_by: Burmese and Chinese operations in 1960 and 1961; evacuation to Taiwan
entries_new.challenge: Government of Burma; People's Republic of China; United Nations pressure
entries_new.mechanism: A displaced army held border hills with outside supply and opium revenue.
entries_new.story: In late 1949 and early 1950 troops of the Republic of China army under Lieutenant-General Li Mi crossed from Yunnan into Burma after losing the Chinese Civil War. They made several raids into Yunnan, were pushed back each time, and from late 1952 spread out across the Shan States and part of Kachin State. The area became Burma's main opium-producing region, and the troops took part in the opium trade, according to Wikipedia. Burma appealed to the United Nations in 1953. Li Mi announced the army's dissolution on 30 May 1954, but about 6,000 irregulars stayed until Burmese and Chinese operations in 1960 and 1961.

entries_new.name: Tambov Rebellion and Antonov's peasant army
entries_new.mechanism: Peasants replaced local Soviet authority with their own union and armed bands.
entries_new.story: Beginning in August 1920 peasants in Tambov governorate, about 500 km southeast of Moscow, resisted forced grain requisitions. Led by Alexander Antonov, a Left Socialist-Revolutionary, and organised through the Union of Working Peasants, they abolished Soviet institutions in the areas they held. By October 1920 the Bolsheviks controlled little of the countryside beyond Tambov city. In May 1921 a Red Army force of 50,000 to 100,000 under Tukhachevsky moved in, and on 12 June 1921 chemical weapons use against rebels in forests was authorised. Antonov was killed on 24 June 1922. Wikipedia cites estimates of about 100,000 arrested and 15,000 killed.

entries_new.name: Quilombo do Leblon, Rio de Janeiro
entries_new.mechanism: A landowner hid escaped slaves on a flower farm with the help of abolitionists and a princess's protection.
entries_new.story: In the late 19th century a quilombo, a settlement of escaped enslaved people, existed in what is now the Leblon district of Rio de Janeiro, between today's Rua Timothy da Costa and Morro Dois Irmaos. It was created by the Portuguese-born luggage maker Jose de Seixas Magalhaes, who grew flowers on a farm there with the help of fugitives and hid them with the aid of leading abolitionists. The farm took its name from an earlier owner, the Frenchman Carlos Leblon, and gave the neighbourhood its name. Seixas supplied camellias to Princess Isabel, who is said to have protected the quilombo and signed the Golden Law on 13 May 1888.

entries_new.name: Insurgent-held Mocimboa da Praia, Cabo Delgado
entries_new.founder: Ansar al-Sunna; Islamic State Central Africa Province
entries_new.mechanism: An insurgent group held a port town and nearby islands and declared the town a provincial capital.
entries_new.story: The Cabo Delgado insurgency in northern Mozambique began in 2017 around Ansar al-Sunna, a group that formed hidden camps in Macomia, Mocimboa da Praia and Montepuez districts and later became linked to the Islamic State's Central Africa Province. On 11 August 2020 insurgents took the port town of Mocimboa da Praia after an offensive that Wikipedia says killed over one hundred Mozambican troops. On 8 September 2020 they captured the islands of Mecungo and Vamizi, evicted local residents, and the Islamic State side declared Mocimboa da Praia its province's capital. Rwandan and Mozambican forces retook the town on 8 August 2021, after most insurgents had left.
entries_new.anchor: Mocimboa da Praia, Cabo Delgado, Mozambique

entries_new.name: Sarbadar state of Sabzavar
entries_new.currency: Coins minted, first in the name of Togha Temur
entries_new.challenge: Ilkhanid claimants, Togha Temur, Chobanids, Timur
entries_new.mechanism: A local rising took towns and ruled by rotating leaders under nominal overlords.
entries_new.story: The Sarbadars (Persian for 'head on gallows') ruled part of western Khurasan from 1337, as the Mongol Ilkhanate broke up, with their capital at Sabzavar. Their rulers were a mix of secular leaders and dervishes (members of a mystic religious order), who sometimes shared power and often fell out. Wikipedia describes the government as something like an oligarchy or republic with no dynastic line, and none of the rulers claimed legitimate sovereignty. They sometimes accepted Mongol claimants as overlord for convenience. About 1340 they defeated the Ja'un Qurban and the khan Togha Temur and took Gurgan. The last ruler, Khwaja Ali Mu'ayyad, submitted to Timur in 1381.

entries_new.name: Second Servile War in Sicily
entries_new.mechanism: Rebel slave kings held fortified towns using captured Roman arms.
entries_new.story: From 104 to 100 BC enslaved people on Sicily rose against the Roman Republic. The trigger was an order that slaves from Rome's allies be freed: the governor Publius Licinius Nerva freed about 800 people, then revoked it. A former slave called Salvius, who took the name Tryphon, defeated Roman forces, took Morgantina and led an army reported at 2,000 horsemen and 20,000 foot soldiers. Athenion, a Cilician slave, led a second rising in the west and later succeeded Salvius as king. The consul Manius Aquillius defeated Athenion in 101 BC. Wikipedia says 1,000 survivors were sent to the Rome arena and killed each other instead of fighting.

entries_new.name: Overthrow and annexation of Hawaii, 1893 to 1898
entries_new.challenge: Queen Liliuokalani; the Blount investigation; Hawaiian sovereignty movement
entries_new.mechanism: A coup backed by US naval personnel was followed by annexation through a joint resolution of Congress.
entries_new.story: On 17 January 1893 a Committee of Safety of foreign-born and Hawaiian-born residents of Honolulu overthrew Queen Liliuokalani. The kingdom had no army, and the committee asked the US minister John L. Stevens to land Marines and sailors, which he did. The committee set up the Republic of Hawaii, aiming at annexation. President Cleveland sent James Blount to investigate; his July 1893 report said US diplomats and troops were responsible for the change. A Senate committee under John Tyler Morgan reached a contrary view. President McKinley signed the Newlands Resolution, and annexation took effect on 7 July 1898. A 1993 US Apology Resolution acknowledged US participation.

sources.t: Wikipedia: Overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom

entries_new.name: Anschluss: annexation of Austria by Germany, 1938
entries_new.challenge: Austrian chancellor Schuschnigg; Mexican delegate at the League of Nations; Allied Moscow Declaration
entries_new.mechanism: Threat of invasion forced a change of government, then a law of union and a plebiscite.
entries_new.story: On 12 March 1938 German troops crossed into Austria, after Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg had been pressed to resign and the Nazi Arthur Seyss-Inquart installed in his place. Schuschnigg had called a referendum on Austrian independence for 13 March, which Hitler demanded be cancelled. A law of 13 March made Austria a province called Ostmark, and a controlled plebiscite on 10 April officially recorded 99.7 percent support. On 18 March Germany told the League of Nations; Mexico's delegate protested. The Moscow Declaration of 1943 by the US, Soviet Union and UK later treated the annexation as null.

entries_new.name: Argentine invasion of the Falkland Islands, 1982
entries_new.challenge: United Kingdom; UN Security Council Resolution 502
entries_new.mechanism: Armed seizure of a territory over which two states claim sovereignty.
entries_new.story: On 2 April 1982 Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands, and the next day South Georgia, describing the action as reclaiming its own territory. The United Kingdom, which has held the islands as a Crown colony since 1841, called it an invasion. UN Security Council Resolution 502, adopted 10 to 1 with four abstentions, called for the withdrawal of Argentine forces and avoided the sovereignty question. A British task force arrived, and Argentina surrendered on 14 June after 74 days. The war killed 649 Argentine and 255 British military personnel and 3 islanders. Argentina's 1994 constitution declares the islands part of one of its provinces.

entries_new.name: Chinese annexation of Central Tibet, 1950 to 1951
entries_new.challenge: Tibetan government, then the Dalai Lama from 1959; Central Tibetan Administration
entries_new.mechanism: Military advance followed by a treaty signed in Beijing.
entries_new.story: After the fall of the Qing dynasty, central Tibet governed itself, and by 1917 was de facto independent. The People's Liberation Army crossed the Jinsha River on 6 or 7 October 1950 and had taken Chamdo by 19 October. Tibetan negotiators in Beijing were given a finished text, the Seventeen Point Agreement, and signed it on 23 May 1951 without permission from Lhasa to do so, according to Wikipedia. The Dalai Lama accepted it in October 1951. He fled in 1959 and repudiated it, saying he approved it under duress. China calls the event 'Peaceful Liberation'; the exiled administration calls it an invasion.

entries_new.name: Security Council Resolution 242
entries_new.mechanism: A Security Council text that rejects keeping territory taken in war and ties withdrawal to recognised borders.
entries_new.story: Resolution 242 was adopted unanimously by the UN Security Council on 22 November 1967, after the Six-Day War. Its preamble refers to the inadmissibility of acquiring territory by war. It calls for a just and lasting peace that includes withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict and respect for the sovereignty and secure, recognised boundaries of every state in the area. It was passed under Chapter VI of the Charter, which covers peaceful settlement. Syria accepted it conditionally in 1972. Wikipedia describes it as the basis of later talks and of the Israel-Egypt (1979) and Israel-Jordan (1994) peace treaties.

entries_new.name: Security Council Resolution 478
entries_new.mechanism: A Council decision that an annexation law is void and should not be recognised by other states.
entries_new.story: Resolution 478, adopted on 20 August 1980 by 14 votes to none with the United States abstaining, is the last of seven Security Council resolutions condemning Israel's annexation of East Jerusalem. It condemned the 1980 Jerusalem Law, which declared Jerusalem Israel's complete and united capital, as a violation of international law, and said the Council would not recognise it. It called on member states to withdraw diplomatic missions from the city. Israel rejected the resolution. The US representative called the instruction on embassies not binding. It was not adopted under Chapter VII, though the UN treats findings of illegal situations as binding.

entries_new.name: M23 (AFC-M23) areas of North and South Kivu
entries_new.challenge: Congolese government and army (FARDC); UN peacekeepers; UN Security Council sanctions
entries_new.mechanism: An armed group holding towns and mining areas and running a parallel administration over them.
entries_new.story: The March 23 Movement (M23) was formed in May 2012 by former fighters of the CNDP who had mutinied against the Congolese army. It took Goma, capital of North Kivu, on 20 November 2012, and withdrew after Great Lakes regional pressure; a UN report found Rwanda created and commanded it then. After a renewed offensive from 2022, M23 announced the capture of Goma on 27 January 2025 and of Bukavu on 16 February 2025. In Rubaya it set up a mineral ministry that taxed coltan and issued permits to miners and traders. The DRC and Rwanda signed a peace agreement in Washington on 27 June 2025.

entries_new.name: Ansaru in north-west Nigeria
aka: Vanguard for the Protection of Muslims in Black Africa
entries_new.founder: Khalid Barnawi and Abubakar Adam Kambar
entries_new.mechanism: A militant group using forest camps in a region with existing armed banditry.
entries_new.story: Ansaru is a Nigerian jihadist group that split from Boko Haram and announced in 2012 that it was independent and pledged to al-Qaeda. Wikipedia says it operated around Kano State, carried out kidnappings of foreigners, and stopped activity in 2013 after commanders returned to Boko Haram. It reappeared in 2020. The article says it maintains a presence in Kaduna State local government areas such as Birnin Gwari, Chikun, Igabi and Giwa. The Nigerian military reported attacks on camps linked to the group in February and August 2020. It states an aim of reviving the Sokoto Caliphate.

entries_new.name: General Assembly Resolution 3314, Definition of Aggression
entries_new.mechanism: A General Assembly definition of which state acts count as aggression, including annexation by force.
entries_new.story: Resolution 3314 (XXIX) was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 14 December 1974 as a non-binding recommendation to the Security Council. It separates an act of aggression, which makes a state internationally responsible, from a war of aggression, which is a crime against international peace. Article 3 lists armed invasion or attack, occupation and annexation by force, bombardment, blockade and attacks on another state's armed forces as acts of aggression. It also covers a state allowing others to use its territory for aggression and sending armed irregulars or mercenaries. Critics call its rules on irregulars vague and say it treats only states as responsible parties.

entries_new.name: Sokoto Caliphate
entries_new.stopped_by: British, French and German conquest in 1903
entries_new.challenge: Hausa kingdoms; later European colonial forces
entries_new.mechanism: A religious reform movement conquered neighbouring kingdoms and ruled them as emirates under one caliph.
entries_new.story: The Sokoto Caliphate was a Sunni Muslim state in West Africa founded by Usman dan Fodio in 1804, in the Fulani jihads against the Hausa kingdoms. His followers pledged allegiance to him as Commander of the Faithful after the Hausa king Yunfa attempted to kill him in 1802. By 1808 it controlled Hausaland and nearby states, and it was a loose confederation of over 30 emirates under the Sultan of Sokoto. Wikipedia estimates 10 to 20 million people by 1837. British, French and German forces conquered it in 1903, when the last caliph, Attahiru, was killed. The sultan's title remains.

entries_new.name: Costa Chica of Guerrero, refuge of escaped slaves
entries_new.mechanism: Runaways settled a remote coast and traded labor for the protection of local landholders.
entries_new.story: The Costa Chica is a stretch of Pacific coast in Guerrero, Mexico, running from just south of Acapulco to the Oaxaca border. Wikipedia reports that enslaved Africans who escaped from sugar plantations, mines and ranches elsewhere in colonial Mexico migrated to this isolated region and found refuge. Spanish landholders there gave them protection in return for cheap labor, mostly tending cattle and curing leather. Over time there was significant mixing with Europeans and indigenous people. Today the area has one of Mexico's two main Afro-Mexican populations, concentrated between Marquelia and Cuajinicuilapa, alongside indigenous Amuzgo communities.

entries_new.name: Revolt of Aristonicus (Eumenes III) at Pergamon
entries_new.challenge: Roman Republic and neighbouring Anatolian kingdoms and Greek cities
entries_new.mechanism: A claimant to a bequeathed throne raised a force and offered freedom to slaves and serfs.
entries_new.story: When King Attalus III of Pergamon died in 133 BC he left his kingdom to Rome. Aristonicus, who claimed to be an illegitimate son of the earlier king Eumenes II, took the name Eumenes III and claimed the throne. He seized coastal cities including Samos, Myndus and Colophon and killed the Roman consul Publius Licinius Crassus Dives Mucianus. Turning inland, he promised freedom to slaves and serfs, and was joined by the Stoic philosopher Blossius, who planned a state called Heliopolis. The consul Marcus Perperna defeated him by 129 BC, and he was sent to Rome. How far he was a social revolutionary or a dynastic claimant is uncertain.

entries_new.name: Torre de David (Centro Financiero Confinanzas), Caracas
entries_new.mechanism: Families occupied an abandoned state-held building and ran its services themselves.
entries_new.story: Centro Financiero Confinanzas is an unfinished skyscraper in downtown Caracas whose construction stopped in 1994 during Venezuela's banking crisis. In October 2007 squatters led by ex-convicts occupied it, in a city short of about 400,000 homes. Residents improvised water and electricity, and the tower grew to 700 families, over 2,500 people by 2011, with a peak population of 5,000. Shops, barbershops and an unlicensed dentist operated inside. On 22 July 2014 the government launched 'Operation Zamora 2014' and moved the families to new housing in Cua, finishing by June 2015. The tower stands unfinished.

entries_new.name: Nahr al-Bared refugee camp
entries_new.founder: League of Red Cross Societies, with UNRWA responsible for the old camp
entries_new.mechanism: Camp security left to Palestinian factions under the 1969 Cairo Agreement.
entries_new.story: Nahr al-Bared is a Palestinian refugee camp 16 km from Tripoli in northern Lebanon, set up in December 1949 for people displaced in 1948. Under the 1969 Cairo Agreement the Lebanese Army does not conventionally enter such camps and Palestinian factions provide internal security. On 20 May 2007, after a clash in Tripoli, members of the Fatah al-Islam militant group attacked an army checkpoint at the camp, and the army shelled it. Most residents fled, and the last civilians were evacuated on 24 August. The army took full control on 2 September 2007. About 30,000 displaced Palestinians and descendants live in and around the camp.
